title: Public Benchmarking Claims Guidelines (Performance + Latency/$)
author: Michael Grant
body:
## Purpose
This page defines **required rules and review steps** for any **external** performance-related claims by Redwood Inference, including (but not limited to) the **Latency per Dollar (latency/$)** public benchmark report, blog posts, landing pages, sales decks, social posts, and partner co-marketing.

The intent is to:
- Ensure claims are **accurate, reproducible, and non-misleading**.
- Align Marketing/Sales messaging with the **actual benchmark methodology and statistical uncertainty**.
- Prevent “benchmark theater” (cherry-picked runs, selective regions/models, or unqualified superlatives).

## Scope
Applies to:
- Redwood-hosted results (Hosted API), Dedicated capacity benchmarks, and any “Private-ready” numbers we choose to publish.
- Any comparisons to:
  - Competitors’ hosted APIs or managed endpoints
  - Prior Redwood results (quarter-over-quarter improvements)
  - Industry baselines from public sources

Out of scope:
- Internal-only dashboards and investigations (still should follow good practice, but this page is for **external claims controls**).

## Definitions (required to use consistently)
- **Latency**: Reported as **p50 and p95 end-to-end latency** (client request start to last token for streaming; clearly specify).
- **Throughput**: Tokens/sec or requests/sec; specify whether this is **per replica**, per GPU, or per deployment pool.
- **Cost**: For public reporting, cost must be defined as **the price the customer would pay** under the referenced plan (or explicitly stated “infrastructure cost estimate” if not customer price). Do not mix these.
- **Latency/$**: A derived “production economics” metric intended to reflect **latency achieved per unit spend**. The public report must state the exact formula and units.

### Required “metric hygiene” statement
Every artifact that contains Latency/$ must include a short note:
> “Latency/$ is a derived metric that combines observed latency and the corresponding price/cost assumptions for the benchmark configuration. It is most useful for comparing like-for-like deployment scenarios and workloads.”

## Claim categories and what is allowed
### A) Allowed: descriptive, bounded, and attributable claims
Examples (approved patterns):
- “In our Feb 2025 benchmark (methodology linked), Redwood achieved **X–Y% better latency/$** than baseline configuration A for model family B in region C.”
- “Across the tested regions, Redwood’s p95 latency varied by **±Z% run-to-run** under the fixed workload distribution.”
- “For the tested prompt distribution and concurrency, Model M on Redwood Dedicated produced **N tokens/sec** (p50/p95 latencies shown).”

Constraints:
- Must include **tested model version(s), region(s), workload description, and date window**.
- Must include uncertainty/variance language (see “Variance and confidence language”).

### B) Allowed with constraints: comparative claims vs competitor offerings
Comparisons are permitted only when ALL of the following are true:
1) **Competitor configuration is documented** (public docs or written confirmation) and matches our test scenario as closely as possible.
2) We run identical workloads and measurement windows (or explicitly disclose differences).
3) We do not imply generality beyond what was tested.
4) We include a short **limitations disclaimer**.

Allowed comparative phrasings:
- “On this workload and configuration, Redwood measured **lower p95 latency** than Vendor X in us-east for Model Y.”
- “In our tests, Redwood delivered **higher latency/$** under the specified workload mix; see methodology and confidence notes.”

Not allowed:
- “Redwood is faster than Vendor X” (unqualified)
- “Best-in-class / #1 / industry-leading” unless a Legal-approved substantiation packet exists that covers **market scope, time window, and methodology**.

### C) Allowed: improvements vs prior Redwood benchmarks
You may claim improvements if:
- The methodology is the same (or deltas are disclosed).
- The prior and current results are both published or available for audit.

Allowed phrasing:
- “Compared to our Nov 2024 report, Redwood improved p95 latency/$ by **~12%** for Model family Q in eu-west (same workload; see change log).”

### D) Not allowed: absolute or implied guarantees
Do not publish:
- Guarantees like “always”, “never”, “zero variance”, “no regressions”.
- Any claim that implies customer workloads will match the benchmark without qualification.
- Any claim that implies competitor intent/misconduct (e.g., “Vendor X inflates pricing,” “Vendor Y hides latency”).

## Variance and confidence language (required)
### Minimum statistical disclosure for public tables/charts
For each model/region/config shown publicly, include:
- Number of runs (N)
- p50 and p95 (or explicitly state if using mean/median)
- A variability measure, one of:
  - **95% confidence interval** (preferred) OR
  - **run-to-run variability band** (e.g., “±4% p95 across N runs”)

If the artifact format cannot support all fields (e.g., social post), it must link to the landing page/report where the full disclosure exists.

### Approved uncertainty language
Use language like:
- “Results include run-to-run variability; see confidence bands in the appendix.”
- “Differences within the variability band should not be over-interpreted.”
- “These measurements represent a controlled workload and may differ from production workloads.”

### Prohibited statistical language
- “Statistically proven” (unless reviewed and substantiated)
- “Significant” in the scientific sense unless we have documented tests and thresholds
- Presenting single-run results as representative

### When NOT to make a “winner” call
Do not declare a winner if:
- Confidence intervals overlap materially, or
- Observed deltas are within the pre-defined variance threshold from Perf/Evals, or
- A known anomaly investigation is open (see anomaly triage playbook).

## Disclosures and disclaimers (required blocks)
Every public benchmark artifact must include (or link to) the following disclosures.

### Required: methodology disclosure (short form)
Include a short-form disclosure block:
- Workload type(s) (chat, embeddings, rerank)
- Input distribution summary (prompt length, output length target)
- Concurrency and rate limiting approach
- Caching/batching policy
- Region(s) and date window
- Model name + exact version identifier

### Required: comparability disclaimer
> “Benchmarks reflect the tested workload, configuration, and time window. Real-world performance depends on prompt distribution, concurrency, networking, safety layers, model settings, and deployment choices.”

### Required: pricing/cost disclaimer
If Latency/$ is shown:
> “Latency/$ reflects benchmarked latency and the corresponding pricing/cost assumptions for the tested configuration. Changes to pricing, discounts, or deployment topology may change results.”

### Conditional: competitive comparison disclaimer
If any competitor is named:
> “Competitor results are based on publicly documented configurations or best-effort matching at the time of testing. Vendor offerings may change; results may differ under alternate settings.”

### Prohibited disclosures
Do not disclose:
- Any customer data, customer identifiers, or customer traffic patterns.
- Any internal-only fleet topology details that meaningfully increase security risk.
- Any non-public pricing exceptions (custom discounts, contract terms) unless explicitly approved for release.

## Acceptable comparisons and fairness requirements
### Region and deployment fairness
- Only compare within the **same region** unless the content explicitly frames cross-region differences (and explains why).
- Do not mix Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private unless the comparisons are clearly labeled and explained.

### Configuration parity
Comparisons must maintain parity across:
- Model (same weights/version where applicable)
- Context length and max output settings
- Safety filters / moderation overhead (if applicable; disclose)
- Streaming vs non-streaming semantics

### Cherry-picking controls
Not allowed:
- Selecting only the best region/model points for Redwood while showing a broader set for others.
- Excluding outlier runs without following the documented rerun policy.

Required:
- If points are removed due to anomaly, note it in internal records and ensure the public story is still representative.

## Guidance on charts, tables, and headlines
### Headlines (public-facing)
Headlines must be:
- Specific (“Latency/$ across 9 open models in 5 regions”) rather than absolute (“Fastest inference”).
- Consistent with what the charts support.

### Charts: required footnotes
All benchmark charts must include a footnote with:
- Date window
- Region(s)
- Workload mix
- Variability/confidence note
- Link/QR to full methodology

### Tables: rounding and units
- Always show units (ms, tokens/sec, $/1M tokens, etc.).
- Use consistent rounding rules across vendors/models.
- Do not round in a way that flips ordering for close values; when close, use “within variance” language.

## Approved language bank (copy/paste)
### Explaining Latency/$
- “Latency/$ is a production-economics metric that combines responsiveness and spend, so engineers and procurement can evaluate tradeoffs on a common axis.”
- “We report p50/p95 latency and cost side-by-side; latency/$ is derived from those values for easier comparison under the tested workload.”

### Explaining limitations without undermining credibility
- “Benchmarks are a snapshot; we publish methodology, variance, and refresh cadence so teams can interpret results responsibly.”
- “We designed the workload distribution to be representative of common production patterns, but your mileage may vary; we provide a reproduction guide.”

### Avoiding over-claiming (safe alternative phrasings)
Instead of: “Redwood is the fastest.”
Use: “Redwood delivered lower p95 latency on this workload in these regions.”

Instead of: “50% cheaper.”
Use: “Lower cost per 1M tokens under the benchmarked configuration; see pricing assumptions.”

## Review and approval checklist (required before publishing)
This checklist applies to any external asset containing benchmark numbers (report PDF, landing page, blog, deck, partner kit, press release, social).

### 1) Methodology verification (Perf/Evals)
Owner: Jonas Weber (delegate: Claire Dubois)
- [ ] Workload definition matches the published methodology page
- [ ] Model identifiers and versions are correct
- [ ] Region list is correct and consistent
- [ ] Variance/CI and run counts are present and correct
- [ ] Any anomalies followed the triage playbook and have sign-off

### 2) Cost/pricing verification (Finance + Metering)
Owner: Nadia Rahman (or delegate)
- [ ] Cost columns reflect the stated pricing assumptions
- [ ] No use of confidential discounting or customer-specific pricing
- [ ] Units and rounding rules are consistent

### 3) Reliability and operational safety (SRE)
Owner: Neha Kapoor (delegate: Sean Gallagher)
- [ ] Benchmark windows did not violate production guardrails
- [ ] Results are not from a period with known region degradation unless disclosed

### 4) Messaging compliance (Marketing)
Owner: Camila Reyes (delegate: Ben Carter)
- [ ] Headlines match what the data supports
- [ ] All disclaimers included or linked
- [ ] No prohibited superlatives or implied guarantees
- [ ] CTA language does not imply performance will match without qualification

### 5) Legal review (required for competitor naming and press)
Owner: Michael Grant
- [ ] Competitive comparisons are substantiated and fairly framed
- [ ] Disclosures are sufficient and not misleading
- [ ] Any partner co-marketing text is within approvals
- [ ] Press release language matches approved claims exactly

### Publication rule
No benchmark asset may be published externally until items (1)–(5) are complete. If there is schedule pressure, scope must be reduced (e.g., remove competitor naming) rather than skipping controls.

## Escalations
If there is disagreement on whether a claim is publishable:
1) Perf/Evals + Legal meet within 24 hours to evaluate substantiation.
2) If unresolved, escalate to Camila Reyes (Marketing Exec Sponsor) + Jonas Weber (Methodology Sponsor) for a decision; Legal retains veto for compliance risk.

## Change management
- Any changes to benchmark methodology that affect external interpretation (e.g., caching policy, concurrency distribution, pricing assumptions) require:
  - A versioned update to the methodology page
  - A visible change log entry in the next public refresh
  - Re-review of this claims guideline section if new metrics or comparison types are introduced

## Appendix: quick “do/don’t”
### Do
- Do link to methodology and include variance language.
- Do state what was tested (model/version, region, workload, date window).
- Do use “in our tests / under this workload / for this configuration.”

### Don’t
- Don’t use unqualified “fastest”, “cheapest”, “best”.
- Don’t compare across different regions or deployments without clear framing.
- Don’t publish single-run results or results during known incidents.
